subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Salaam and welcome, young scientist! In this unit you are going to become a materials detective. Every single day, all around you, materials are being mixed together and pulled apart again. When your mother stirs sugar into a hot glass of shaah (tea), she is mixing materials. When you shake sand off your feet after playing at the Indian Ocean beach in Mombasa or Kismaayo, you are separating materials. When Grandmother picks the tiny stones out of the bariis (rice) before cooking, she is separating a mixture. Science is not only found in books and laboratories. It is happening in your own kitchen, at the well, and on the shore.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Science 0846 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Explain what a mixture is and give examples of mixtures from your own home.
Describe what it means for a material to dissolve, and use the word solution correctly.
Predict and test which materials dissolve in water and which do not.
Name and describe four ways to separate mixtures: sieving, filtering, evaporation, and letting things settle (decanting).
Choose the best separation method for a given mixture and explain why it works.
Plan and carry out a fair test, changing only one thing at a time.
Record what you observe carefully and honestly, and draw a sensible conclusion.
Here are the important words for this unit. Read them slowly. You will meet each one again inside the lessons, so do not worry about memorising them all at once.

concepts.title: Everything Is Made From Materials
concepts.explanation:
Before we can mix materials, we must know what a material is. A material is simply what an object is made from. Your spoon is made from metal. Your cup might be made from plastic or clay. The canjeero on your plate is made from flour, water, and a little salt. Water itself is a material. Sand is a material. Sugar and salt are materials. When we talk about mixing, we are talking about putting two or more materials together.

Every material has properties. Properties are the things you notice about a material — its colour, whether it is hard or soft, rough or smooth, whether you can pour it, and whether it dissolves in water. When Amina looks at a handful of dry rice, she notices it is hard, small, and pale. When she looks at cooking oil, she notices it is yellow, slippery, and can be poured. Noticing properties carefully is the first skill of a good scientist.
concepts.example: Materials come in different states. A solid like a stone or a grain of rice holds its own shape. A liquid like water or camel milk flows and takes the shape of whatever container you pour it into. There are also gases, like the air all around us, which spread out to fill any space. In this unit we will mostly mix solids into liquids — like stirring sugar (a solid) into tea (a liquid) — so keep these two states firmly in your mind.

concepts.title: What Is a Mixture?
concepts.explanation:
A mixture is what you get when two or more materials are put together but each material still keeps its own properties. This is a very important idea, so read it again slowly. In a mixture, nothing is destroyed. The materials are simply sitting together, and if you are clever, you can take them apart again.

Imagine Hassan pours a cup of dry bariis (rice) onto a tray and finds some small stones hidden in it. The rice and the stones are now a mixture. The rice is still rice — it has not turned into stone. The stones are still stones. They are just mixed up together. Because each one keeps its own properties (the stones are hard and heavy, the rice is light and edible), Hassan can separate them again by picking the stones out, one by one, the way his grandmother does before every meal.

Here are more mixtures from daily life in East Africa. Sand and small shells on the beach at Lamu are a mixture. Tea leaves floating in hot water are a mixture. A handful of mixed beans and lentils is a mixture. Muddy water from the well, where dust and soil float in the water, is a mixture. Even the air you breathe is a mixture of different gases! Once you understand mixtures, you start to see them everywhere.

Some mixtures are easy to see, and some are harder. In a mixture of rice and beans, you can clearly see the two different materials sitting side by side. We call this a mixture you can see the parts of. But when Khadija stirs salt into water, the salt seems to disappear, and the water still looks clear. You cannot see the separate parts any more — yet the salt is still there, hiding in the water. This special kind of mixture, where a solid disappears into a liquid, has its own name, and that is our next big idea.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The Indian Ocean water at Kismaayo and Mombasa is a giant salty mixture. Sea water is a solution of salt and other minerals in water. If you left a shallow dish of sea water in the hot sun, the water would evaporate and leave real salt crystals behind — the same way sea salt is made!

concepts.title: Dissolving and Solutions
concepts.explanation:
When you stir a spoon of sugar into a hot cup of shaah, something wonderful happens. At first you can see the white grains sitting at the bottom. But as you stir, the grains get smaller and smaller until — they are gone! The sugar has dissolved. Dissolving is when a solid breaks up into pieces so tiny that you cannot see them any more, and they spread evenly all through the liquid.

It is very important to understand this: the sugar has not disappeared from the world. It has not been destroyed. It is still there, floating in tiny hidden pieces throughout the tea. How do we know? Because the whole cup of tea now tastes sweet, from the top to the bottom. Your tongue is the proof that the sugar is still there. When a solid dissolves completely in a liquid like this, the clear mixture we are left with is called a solution. Sweet tea is a solution of sugar in water.

A material that can dissolve is called soluble. Sugar is soluble in water. Salt is soluble in water. A material that does not dissolve is called insoluble. Sand is insoluble — stir it into water as long as you like and it will always sink back to the bottom, still as sand. Cooking oil is insoluble too — it floats on top of water in a separate yellow layer and never mixes in. Flour is only partly soluble; it makes the water go cloudy and slowly sinks, which is why canjeero batter must be stirred and is thick and cloudy, not clear.

So, why do some things dissolve and others do not? At the tiniest level, water is very good at pulling apart the pieces of sugar and salt and surrounding each tiny piece. But water cannot pull apart the pieces of sand or oil, so those materials stay whole and separate. You do not need to remember all the tiny details yet — just remember the pattern: sugar and salt dissolve, sand and oil do not.

Sometimes a solid dissolves quickly, and sometimes it takes a long time. Three things change the speed of dissolving, and you can test each one at home:

Heat. Sugar dissolves much faster in hot tea than in cold water. The warmer the liquid, the faster the dissolving. This is why your mother adds sugar while the tea is still hot.

Stirring. When you stir with a spoon, the solid dissolves faster. Stirring moves the tiny pieces away and lets fresh water reach the solid. If you never stir, dissolving takes much longer.

Grain size. A spoon of fine, powdery sugar dissolves faster than one big lump of sugar. Smaller pieces have more surface touching the water, so they break apart more quickly.
concepts.example: Understanding these three helpers — heat, stirring, and small grains — lets you dissolve things quickly when you want to, and it also teaches you how to plan a careful fair test, which you will learn about soon.

concepts.title: Separating Mixtures
concepts.explanation:
Because a mixture is only materials sitting together, we can nearly always pull them apart again. This is called separating a mixture. The clever part of science is choosing the right method for each mixture. The method you choose depends on how the materials are different from each other — are they different sizes? Is one a solid floating in a liquid? Is one dissolved? Let us look at four important methods, all of which you can try safely at home.

A sieve is a tool with many small holes, like the kitchen sieve your family uses for flour. Small pieces fall through the holes, while big pieces are too large and stay behind. Sieving works when the materials in your mixture are different sizes.

For example, imagine Maryam has a bowl of flour with hard lumps in it. She pours it through a sieve. The fine, soft flour falls through the little holes into the bowl below, but the big lumps cannot fit through the holes, so they are left behind in the sieve. Now she has smooth flour ready for baking. Farmers use giant sieves to separate grain from bits of stalk, and builders sieve sand to remove pebbles before mixing cement.

Method 2: Filtering (Solid Out of a Liquid)

Filtering means pouring a mixture through a cloth or paper that has holes far too small to see. The liquid trickles through the tiny holes, but solid pieces that are floating in the liquid are caught and left behind. Filtering is perfect for taking solid bits out of a liquid.

Think about muddy water carried up from the well. It is a mixture of water and tiny bits of soil. If Yusuf pours this muddy water slowly through a clean, folded cloth, the water passes through and comes out much clearer, while the mud and dirt stay trapped in the cloth. Filtering does not make water safe to drink all by itself — the water must still be boiled to kill germs — but filtering is an important first step to remove the dirt you can see. This is real, life-saving science used across East Africa.

Method 3: Evaporation (Getting a Dissolved Solid Back)

What if a solid has dissolved and you cannot see it any more? A sieve is useless — the salt in salty water is far too small to catch. A filter is useless too — the dissolved salt slips straight through with the water. To get a dissolved solid back, we use evaporation.

When a liquid is left in a warm, sunny place, it slowly turns into a gas (water vapour) and floats away into the air. This is called evaporating. But here is the clever part: the dissolved solid cannot evaporate. It is left behind! So if Zahra leaves a shallow dish of salty water in the hot sun, day after day the water evaporates until, at last, only dry salt crystals remain in the dish. The water has gone into the air, but the salt could not follow it, so it stayed. This is exactly how people have made salt from sea water for thousands of years along the coasts of the Indian Ocean.

Some heavy solids do not dissolve and simply sink to the bottom if you leave the mixture still. This is called settling. When Idris brings home a bucket of muddy water and lets it stand quietly for a few hours, the heavy soil slowly sinks and gathers at the bottom, while cleaner water rises to the top. Then he can carefully pour off the clear water on top into another container, leaving the mud behind. Pouring off the clear liquid gently like this is called decanting. Settling and decanting are often used before filtering, to remove the heaviest dirt first.

Now you know four methods. The secret to being a good materials detective is asking: How are these materials different? If they are different sizes, sieve them. If a solid is floating in a liquid, filter it. If a solid is dissolved, evaporate the liquid. If a heavy solid can sink, let it settle and decant. Match the method to the mixture, and you can separate almost anything.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The way you clean muddy well water at home — settle, then filter, then boil — is a small version of what huge water-treatment plants do for whole cities. Engineers use the very same ideas of settling, filtering, and cleaning, just with enormous tanks. The science you learn in your kitchen is the same science that keeps a city healthy.

concepts.title: Being a Fair Scientist (Fair Tests)
concepts.explanation:
When scientists want to find something out, they do a fair test. A fair test is an investigation where you change only one thing and keep everything else exactly the same. This is the only way to be sure what caused your result. If you change many things at once, you can never be certain which change made the difference.

Imagine Sahra wants to find out whether sugar dissolves faster in hot water or cold water. To be fair, she must use the same amount of sugar in each cup, the same amount of water in each cup, and stir the same number of times. The only thing she is allowed to change is the temperature of the water — hot in one cup, cold in the other. Now, if the sugar dissolves faster in the hot cup, she knows for certain that the heat made the difference, because heat was the only thing she changed.
concepts.example: In a fair test there are three kinds of things to think about. The thing you change on purpose (here, the temperature). The thing you measure or watch (here, how long the sugar takes to dissolve). And the things you keep the same to be fair (the amount of sugar, the amount of water, and the stirring). Good scientists plan all three before they begin. Doing this makes your discoveries trustworthy — and being truthful and careful is a value that Islam praises highly.

concepts.title: Some Changes Can Be Undone
concepts.explanation:
Here is a thought that surprises many young scientists. When you mix materials or dissolve them, you have not made a brand-new substance. You have only put things together, and most of the time you can take them apart again and get the very same materials back. A change that you can undo like this is called a reversible change. Mixing and dissolving are both reversible changes, and this is exactly why separating works so well.

Think about the salt experiment. When Zahra dissolves salt in water, she seems to lose the salt. But by evaporating the water, she gets her salt back, exactly as it was. Nothing was destroyed and nothing new was made. The change was reversed. In the same way, when Grandmother mixes rice and beans, she can un-mix them; when Yusuf muddies water with soil, he can settle and filter it clean again. Because these changes are reversible, the materials never lose their own properties.

Not every change in the world is reversible, though. When bread dough is baked into canjeero over the fire, or when an egg is cooked, you cannot turn it back into the runny batter or the raw egg again. Those are irreversible changes, and they make a truly new material. But in this unit, the mixing, dissolving, and separating you study are all reversible — and that is the good news that makes a materials detective's job possible. If mixing destroyed materials forever, no one could ever separate them.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Melting and freezing are reversible too. When ice melts into water and then freezes back into ice, it is still the same water all along. Water can change between solid, liquid, and gas again and again without ever being destroyed.

methods.title: What Dissolves in Water?
methods.example: To find out which everyday materials are soluble (dissolve) and which are insoluble (do not dissolve) in water. Make a Prediction Before you start, write down your guess: Which of these do you think will dissolve — sugar, salt, sand, flour, cooking oil? Guessing first is what real scientists do.
steps: Fill each of the five cups with the same amount of cool water.
Add one small spoon of sugar to the first cup and stir ten times. Watch closely.
Do the same with salt, sand, flour, and oil — one material per cup, stirring each ten times.
Wait one minute, then look at each cup. Has the material disappeared, sunk, floated, or made the water cloudy?
Record what you see for each cup in the table below.

methods.title: The Great Dissolving Race (A Fair Test)
methods.example: To find out whether sugar dissolves faster in warm water or in cool water, using a fair test. Make a Prediction Which cup do you think will win the race — warm or cool? Write your guess and one reason why.
steps: Fill one glass with warm water and the other with the same amount of cool water.
Add exactly one level spoon of sugar to each glass at the same moment.
Stir each glass the same number of times — for example, ten stirs each.
Watch and time how long the sugar takes to fully disappear in each glass.
Record both times in your notebook.

methods.title: Cleaning Muddy Water (Settle and Filter)
methods.example: To separate dirt from muddy water using settling and filtering, just like cleaning well water at home. Make a Prediction Do you think letting the water stand still will help? Do you think a cloth will make it clearer? Write your guesses.
steps: Stir the soil into the water to make muddy water. Look at how cloudy it is.
Let the jar stand completely still for ten minutes. Watch what the heavy soil does.
Gently pour the clearer water from the top into a second jar, leaving the settled mud behind. This is decanting.
Now fold the clean cloth over the second jar and slowly pour the water through it. This is filtering.
Compare the final water with the muddy water you started with.

methods.title: Getting the Salt Back (Evaporation)
methods.example: To get dissolved salt back out of salty water by evaporation — proving the salt never really disappeared. Make a Prediction When all the water dries up, what will be left in the dish? Write your prediction.
steps: Stir the salt into the warm water until it dissolves completely and the water looks clear.
Pour a thin layer of this salty water into the shallow dish.
Place the dish in a warm, sunny spot where no one will disturb it.
Each day, look at the dish. Watch the water level slowly drop as it evaporates.
When all the water has gone, look closely at what is left behind.

methods.title: Sieving to Separate by Size
methods.example: To separate a mixture of two different-sized materials using a sieve. Make a Prediction Which material will fall through the holes, and which will stay behind? Why?
steps: Look at your mixture and notice that it has two different sizes of material.
Hold the sieve over the bowl and pour the mixture into the sieve.
Gently shake the sieve from side to side.
Watch which material falls through into the bowl, and which stays in the sieve.
Record your results.

workedExamples.title: A Fair Test, Step by Step
workedExamples.prompt: Let us walk through a real fair test together, the way a careful scientist would, so you can see every step. Our question is: Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water or in cold water?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Ask the question. We want to compare hot water and cold water for dissolving sugar.

Step 2 — Make a prediction. Sahra predicts the sugar will dissolve faster in the hot water, because she has seen sugar vanish quickly in hot tea.

Step 3 — Decide what to change. We change only one thing: the temperature of the water. One cup has warm water (safe to touch, never boiling), the other has cool water.

Step 4 — Decide what to keep the same. To be fair, both cups get exactly one level spoon of sugar, exactly the same amount of water, and we stir each one ten times in the same way.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: What is a mixture? (a) One material alone (b) Two or more materials together, each keeping its properties (c) A brand-new material (d) Only liquids
workedExamples.solution: 1. (b) — A mixture is two or more materials together, and each one keeps its own properties.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: When sugar dissolves in tea, the sugar: (a) disappears forever (b) turns into water (c) breaks into tiny pieces spread through the tea (d) sinks and stays at the bottom
workedExamples.solution: 2. (c) — The sugar breaks into pieces too small to see and spreads through the tea; it is not destroyed.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: A material that dissolves in water is called: (a) insoluble (b) soluble (c) solid (d) magnetic
workedExamples.solution: 3. (b) — A material that dissolves is soluble.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is insoluble in water? (a) sugar (b) salt (c) sand (d) nothing
workedExamples.solution: 4. (c) — Sand is insoluble; it sinks and never dissolves. Sugar and salt do dissolve.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: The clear liquid made when a solid dissolves completely is a: (a) mixture of stones (b) solution (c) sieve (d) filter
workedExamples.solution: 5. (b) — A solution is the clear liquid formed when a solid dissolves completely.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: To separate stones from rice, the best method is: (a) evaporation (b) filtering (c) sieving or picking by size (d) boiling
workedExamples.solution: 6. (c) — Stones and rice are different sizes, so sieving (or picking) separates them.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: To get dissolved salt back from salty water, you should use: (a) a sieve (b) a magnet (c) evaporation (d) a filter
workedExamples.solution: 7. (c) — Dissolved salt is too tiny to sieve or filter, so we evaporate the water and leave the salt behind.

activities.title: What Dissolves in Water?
activities.materials: 5 clear cups or glasses of water; A small spoon of each: sugar, salt, sand (or soil), flour, cooking oil; A stirring spoon; Your notebook and a pencil
steps: Fill each of the five cups with the same amount of cool water.
Add one small spoon of sugar to the first cup and stir ten times. Watch closely.
Do the same with salt, sand, flour, and oil — one material per cup, stirring each ten times.
Wait one minute, then look at each cup. Has the material disappeared, sunk, floated, or made the water cloudy?
Record what you see for each cup in the table below.

activities.title: The Great Dissolving Race (A Fair Test)
activities.materials: 2 clear glasses the same size; Warm water (safe to touch) and cool water; 2 level spoons of sugar; A clock or a way to count slowly; Your notebook
steps: Fill one glass with warm water and the other with the same amount of cool water.
Add exactly one level spoon of sugar to each glass at the same moment.
Stir each glass the same number of times — for example, ten stirs each.
Watch and time how long the sugar takes to fully disappear in each glass.
Record both times in your notebook.

activities.title: Cleaning Muddy Water (Settle and Filter)
activities.materials: A cup of clean water mixed with a spoon of soil or sand (your 'muddy water'); 2 clean jars or cups; A clean cotton cloth or a coffee filter; A spoon
steps: Stir the soil into the water to make muddy water. Look at how cloudy it is.
Let the jar stand completely still for ten minutes. Watch what the heavy soil does.
Gently pour the clearer water from the top into a second jar, leaving the settled mud behind. This is decanting.
Now fold the clean cloth over the second jar and slowly pour the water through it. This is filtering.
Compare the final water with the muddy water you started with.

activities.title: Getting the Salt Back (Evaporation)
activities.materials: A spoon of salt; A cup of warm water; A shallow dish or plate (dark colours show salt best); A sunny windowsill or warm, safe spot; Patience — this takes 1 to 3 days!
steps: Stir the salt into the warm water until it dissolves completely and the water looks clear.
Pour a thin layer of this salty water into the shallow dish.
Place the dish in a warm, sunny spot where no one will disturb it.
Each day, look at the dish. Watch the water level slowly drop as it evaporates.
When all the water has gone, look closely at what is left behind.

activities.title: Sieving to Separate by Size
activities.materials: A kitchen sieve or a clean cloth with small holes; A mixture of two sizes, such as flour with a few dry beans in it, or rice mixed with a spoon of salt; A bowl to catch the small pieces; Your notebook
steps: Look at your mixture and notice that it has two different sizes of material.
Hold the sieve over the bowl and pour the mixture into the sieve.
Gently shake the sieve from side to side.
Watch which material falls through into the bowl, and which stays in the sieve.
Record your results.

activities.title: Observe: Some Changes Can Be Undone
activities.materials: 5 clear cups or glasses of water; A small spoon of each: sugar, salt, sand (or soil), flour, cooking oil; A stirring spoon; Your notebook and a pencil
steps: Look for an example of some changes can be undone around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Method and Sieving.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Key idea 1
rules.text: Filtering removes bits of dirt you can see, but it does NOT remove tiny germs. Water must always be boiled after filtering before it is safe to drink. Boiling and clean water protect your family from sickness. This is science that keeps you healthy.

rounds.prompt: Filtering muddy water makes it look clean, but before drinking it you must still:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Filtering removes visible dirt, but germs remain, so the water must be boiled.

rounds.prompt: A material that dissolves in water is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A material that dissolves is soluble.

rounds.prompt: To separate stones from rice, the best method is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Stones and rice are different sizes, so sieving (or picking) separates them.

rounds.prompt: Sugar dissolves faster when the water is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Warmer water makes a solid dissolve faster.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can explain what a mixture is and give examples of mixtures from your own home.
I can describe what it means for a material to dissolve, and use the word solution correctly.
I can predict and test which materials dissolve in water and which do not.
I can name and describe four ways to separate mixtures: sieving, filtering, evaporation, and letting things settle (decanting).
I can choose the best separation method for a given mixture and explain why it works.
I can plan and carry out a fair test, changing only one thing at a time.
I can record what you observe carefully and honestly, and draw a sensible conclusion.
